title: A Robot Bird That Can Fly and Swim
summary:
Atlantic puffins do more than fly. They also use their wings to swim underwater and chase food. Now, scientists at MIT have built a robot bird that does the same thing. The team was led by Raphael Zufferey.

The robot is called the FAAV. It uses its wings to move between air and water. That is hard because water is about 1,000 times denser than air, so moving through water takes much more force. The team gave the robot bendy wings that flex up to 90 degrees in water. They tested three wing sizes; medium wings worked best. The wings were also coated with tiny bits that push water away, so they stay light.

In tests, the robot swam at nearly 3 feet (1 meter) per second and flew at about 20 feet (6 meters) per second, as fast as real diving birds. It took off from the water using only its wings, without paddling its feet. The team shared its work in the journal Science on July 9, 2026. One day, the robot could help scientists study the ocean.
why_it_matters: It shows how copying animals can help inventors build machines that explore places you may one day study or visit.

background_read: Some real seabirds, like puffins, use their wings to both fly in the air and swim underwater.
Building a machine that can do both is hard because water is much thicker than air, so wings need a special shape to work in both places.
Scientists copy ideas from nature to build robots that may one day help explore the ocean.
